mcqs.question: Why must wait() on a condition variable atomically release the mutex and block, rather than doing those as two separate steps?
options: Because separate steps would use more memory
Because the mutex would otherwise never be re-acquired afterward
Atomicity here is only a performance optimization, not a correctness requirement
Because if the mutex were released before blocking is registered, another thread could change the condition and signal in that gap, and the wakeup would be lost
mcqs.explanation: The atomicity closes exactly the gap where another thread could change the condition and signal before this thread is actually registered as waiting, which would cause a lost wakeup since an unheard signal isn't remembered. This is a correctness issue, not a memory or performance detail, and re-acquisition on wakeup is a separate, guaranteed part of wait()'s contract.

mcqs.question: In the producer-consumer code shown, why does the code use two separate condition variables (not_full, not_empty) instead of one?
options: Because pthreads requires a minimum of two condition variables per mutex
Each condition variable expresses a distinct predicate over the shared state, so signaling one doesn't wake threads waiting on an unrelated condition
One condition variable is reserved for producers only by convention, with no functional difference
Two condition variables run on separate CPU cores for better performance
mcqs.explanation: Using one condition variable per distinct predicate avoids waking threads whose condition hasn't actually changed — signaling not_empty only wakes consumers, not producers waiting on a completely different predicate. There's no such pthreads minimum, no separate-core execution model for condition variables, and the split isn't just convention — it changes which threads get woken.

mcqs.question: Why should wait() on a condition variable always be wrapped in a while loop instead of an if statement?
options: A while loop is required by the C language syntax for condition variables
Spurious wakeups and Mesa-semantics signaling mean the condition might not actually be true when the thread resumes, so it must be rechecked
An if statement would cause a compiler error
The while loop makes the code run on multiple threads simultaneously
mcqs.explanation: Both spurious wakeups (permitted by POSIX) and the fact that a signaled condition can become false again before this thread actually gets the mutex (under Mesa semantics) mean waking up is not a guarantee the condition holds. The while loop rechecks and re-waits if needed. There's no such syntax requirement or compiler error, and looping doesn't parallelize anything.

mcqs.question: Under Mesa monitor semantics (used by pthreads, Java, and Windows), what is guaranteed to a thread the moment it wakes up from wait()?
options: The condition it was waiting for is guaranteed to still be true
It is guaranteed to run immediately with no other thread intervening
Only that it is now eligible to compete for the mutex again — the condition must still be rechecked
It is guaranteed to be the only thread that was signaled
mcqs.explanation: Mesa semantics only promises the woken thread becomes ready to re-acquire the mutex — it makes no guarantee the condition is still true, or that no other thread ran first, or that it was the only one woken (broadcast can wake several). That's exactly why the while-loop recheck is mandatory under Mesa semantics.

mcqs.question: A task queue has 50 threads blocked waiting for a single freed slot, and the code calls broadcast() every time one slot frees up. What production problem does this likely cause?
options: A deadlock, since broadcast() can only be called once per condition variable
The condition variable silently drops most of the wakeups
No problem at all, since broadcast() is always more correct than signal()
A thundering herd — all 50 threads wake and contend for the mutex, but only one can proceed, wasting most of the wakeups
mcqs.explanation: Waking all 50 waiters when only one slot is available means 49 threads wake, contend for the mutex, find the condition false again, and go back to sleep — the thundering herd pattern, which wastes CPU and increases lock contention. broadcast() being correct (with a while-loop recheck) doesn't mean it's the efficient choice here; signal() would wake exactly the one thread that can proceed. There's no deadlock or dropped-wakeup behavior implied.
